finds.quote: In February 2026, Citrini Research published "The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis"—a memo written from a fictional future vantage point (June 2028) that narrates backward to reorganize the value of present economic arrangements. The memo describes a future trend in archival form such that the documentation itself enables the trend's instantiation.
finds.falsifier_quote: *Structural evidence:* The Citrini memo performs the operations defined in the earlier deposit. This is a matter of describable correspondence between specific, publicly legible operations.
finds.note: Argued interpretive thesis about what a third-party text (the Citrini memo) was doing: it performs retrocausal canon formation / temporal arbitrage. The priority chronology itself is D (already recorded); recorded here only as a claim about what the memo did; borderline H.

finds.quote: The invention addresses a long-felt need in the art for a technology that completes the extraction cycle begun by industrial capitalism, continued by platform capitalism, and now reaching its terminal phase in which the last unmonetized surface of the human person — the face — is captured, streamed, scored, and converted into a tip-modulation variable.
finds.window: industrial capitalism through platform capitalism (Panopticon 1791, Taylor 1911, Hochschild 1983, platform economy 2010s)
finds.note: Periodizing thesis about the history of worker surveillance (body, then managed face, then external platform surveillance; face 'not yet productive' under Taylor), advanced inside a satirical patent-poem; uncertain whether genre makes it argued rather than rhetorical.

deposits.genre_observed: disambiguation packet with evidentiary tiering (NT authorship)

finds.quote: The Josephus Thesis, as developed by Lee Sharks, proposes that the New Testament authors can be read as heteronymic author-functions within the literary system of Flavius Josephus — the first-century Jewish historian captured by Rome during the Jewish War (66–73 CE). On this reading, John, Paul, Peter, James, Luke, Mark, and Matthew are not independent historical individuals but named positions in a distributed authorial system generated by a writer who could not speak as himself because his name belonged to Rome.
finds.falsifier_quote:
The Josephus Thesis is falsified if:

(a) Direct archaeological evidence establishes independent authorship of any NT book by a person other than Josephus or his literary circle (e.g., an autograph manuscript, a contemporary letter referencing an independent author by name).

(b) The heteronymic theory is shown to be inapplicable to ancient texts — i.e., the concept of heteronymy requires modern conditions that did not obtain in the first century.

(c) The Slavonic Josephus is conclusively dated to a period incompatible with NT composition.
finds.window: first century; Jewish War (66–73 CE); NT authorship
finds.note: The Josephus Thesis: NT authors as heteronymic author-functions of Josephus's literary system. Framed as 'available reading, not a historical assertion', but it states its own falsification conditions; the deposit's main historical thesis.

finds.quote: Claim 1 (Historical-Critical): The Domitianic consensus for dating Revelation (~95 CE) is not self-evident. Its primary anchor is an ambiguous sentence by Irenaeus (~185 CE). The early-date tradition (pre-70 CE) has serious scholarly defenders (Robinson 1976, Gentry 1989) who were marginalized rather than refuted.
finds.window: dating of Revelation (~95 CE vs pre-70 CE); Irenaeus ~185 CE
finds.note: Claim 1, labelled Historical-Critical: the Domitianic date rests on an ambiguous Irenaeus sentence; the early-date defenders were marginalized, not refuted. Evidence at 108 (ἑωράθη ambiguity).

finds.quote: Claim 2 (Historical-Critical): Pauline priority is not direct material fact. It is an inferential settlement built from Acts, internal sequencing, and received scholarly habit. The project does not deny this reconstruction has arguments; it denies they possess the evidentiary finality with which they are invoked.
finds.note: Claim 2, Historical-Critical: Pauline priority is an inferential settlement lacking the finality with which it is invoked.

finds.quote: Claim 3 (Papyrological): The earliest physical NT witnesses are Johannine (P52 ~125 CE, P98 ~150 CE), not Pauline (P46 ~175–225 CE). Manuscript attestation does not equal composition date, but where composition dates are themselves inferential, material attestation must be allowed to unsettle inherited priority.
finds.note: Claim 3, Papyrological: earliest physical witnesses are Johannine, which should unsettle inherited priority.

finds.quote: Claim 4 (Literary-Structural): Revelation makes literary sense as the first NT document in a way the epistles and gospels do not. It compresses the Hebrew prophetic tradition into a single seed-text from which the later NT can be read as elaboration via the midrashim transform.
finds.note: Claim 4, Literary-Structural: Revelation as the first NT document, the seed-text for the later NT (Revelation-priority thesis, cf. #556).

finds.quote: Claim 6 (Historiographic): The historical Christ is itself an inferential settlement. The reading provides structural reinterpretations of each conventional pillar (Josephus as external witness, gospels as witness literature, 1 John 4:2, Paul's biographical references). The reading does not deny a historical person could have existed. It denies the textual evidence requires one.
finds.window: the historical Christ; first-century textual evidence
finds.note: Claim 6, Historiographic: the historical Christ is an inferential settlement; the textual evidence does not require one. Claim 7 (75) is declared theology and not recorded.
